questions.q: What happened to PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) in Kubernetes, and why?
options: It was renamed to NetworkPolicy and merged into the networking API group
It was deprecated in 1.21 and removed in 1.25 because its RBAC-based policy-to-Pod matching was confusing and error-prone
It is still the current, recommended mechanism and was never deprecated
It was replaced by requiring every cluster to install OPA Gatekeeper before any Pod could be scheduled
questions.explain: PSP was deprecated in Kubernetes 1.21 and fully removed in 1.25. It worked, but policies were bound to Pods through RBAC in a way that was hard to reason about and easy to misconfigure.

questions.q: Which of the three Pod Security Standards levels is correctly described?
options: Baseline requires runAsNonRoot and a seccompProfile on every container
Privileged is the strictest level and blocks all host namespace access
Restricted is the strictest level and additionally requires runAsNonRoot, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, and dropped capabilities
Restricted and Baseline enforce identical rules; only the name differs
questions.explain: Restricted layers on top of Baseline: non-root execution, no privilege escalation, dropped Linux capabilities, and a seccomp profile. Privileged is actually the unrestricted level, and Baseline alone does not require runAsNonRoot.

questions.q: How does Pod Security Admission (PSA) decide which Pod Security Standard to enforce for a given Pod?
options: It reads pod-security.kubernetes.io/ labels set on that Pod's namespace
It scans the Pod's container image for a label embedded by the image's build process
It reads a cluster-wide ConfigMap named psp-replacement that lists every allowed Pod spec
Every Pod is evaluated against all three standards simultaneously with no way to choose one
questions.explain: PSA is a built-in admission controller that reads enforce/audit/warn labels set on the namespace, each naming a standard (privileged, baseline, or restricted) to apply to Pods created in it.

questions.q: What's the practical difference between setting a namespace's `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce` label versus its `warn` label?
options: `enforce` only applies to Deployments, while `warn` only applies to bare Pods
They behave identically; `warn` is simply the deprecated name for `enforce`
`enforce` rejects a violating Pod outright, while `warn` lets it through but prints a client-side warning — useful for rolling out a stricter standard safely
`warn` deletes the violating Pod automatically after 30 seconds, while `enforce` only logs it
questions.explain: enforce actually blocks creation of a non-compliant Pod. warn (and audit) let it through while surfacing the violation, which is how teams test a stricter standard before flipping enforce on for real.

questions.q: According to the lesson, when does a cluster typically add a policy engine like OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno on top of Pod Security Admission?
options: Never — PSA and a policy engine are mutually exclusive and cannot run in the same cluster
Only when running on a cloud provider that doesn't support PSA natively
When rules need to be more specific than PSA's three fixed profiles, such as requiring images from one specific internal registry
Only to replace etcd encryption at rest
questions.explain: PSA enforces exactly three fixed profiles with no concept of org-specific rules like approved registries or required labels. A policy engine plugs in as an admission webhook to add those custom constraints alongside PSA.
